section.title: The Good Shepherd
section.sectionRationale: Flowing out of the expulsion of the healed man by false shepherds, Jesus presents Himself as the true shepherd of God's flock. He is both the gate through which the sheep are saved and the good shepherd who lays down His life for them. At the winter Feast of Dedication the theme sharpens into a confrontation over His identity, culminating in the claim, I and the Father are one, and the promise that no one can snatch His sheep from His hand.
section.thesis: Jesus is the door by which the sheep are saved and the good shepherd who willingly lays down His life and takes it up again for His flock, gathering one flock from many folds, so that His sheep hear His voice, follow Him, receive eternal life, and can never be snatched from the hand of the Son who is one with the Father.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the parable of the sheepfold and the true shepherd's voice; I am the gate and I am the good shepherd who lays down His life; the division His words cause; and, at the Feast of Dedication, the security of the sheep and the claim I and the Father are one, met with stones.

verses.text: “Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever does not enter the sheepfold by the gate, but climbs in some other way, is a thief and a robber.
But the one who enters by the gate is the shepherd of the sheep.
The gatekeeper opens the gate for him, and the sheep listen for his voice. He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out.
When he has brought out all his own, he goes on ahead of them, and his sheep follow him because they know his voice.
But they will never follow a stranger; in fact, they will flee from him because they do not recognize his voice.”
Jesus spoke to them using this illustration, but they did not understand what He was telling them.

units.label: I am the gate and the good shepherd
units.note: the shepherd lays down His life

verses.text: So He said to them again, “Truly, truly, I tell you, I am the gate for the sheep.
All who came before Me were thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them.
{{egoeimi|I am}} the {{thura|gate}}. If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved. He will come in and go out and find pasture.
The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I have come that they may have life, and have it in all its fullness.
I am the {{poimen|good shepherd}}. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep.
The hired hand is not the shepherd, and the sheep are not his own. When he sees the wolf coming, he abandons the sheep and runs away. Then the wolf pounces on them and scatters the flock.
The man runs away because he is a hired servant and is unconcerned for the sheep.
I am the good shepherd. I know My sheep and My sheep know Me,
just as the Father knows Me and I know the Father. And I lay down My life for the sheep.
I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them in as well, and they will listen to My voice. Then there will be one flock and one shepherd.
The reason the Father loves Me is that I lay down My life in order to take it up again.
No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord. I have authority to lay it down and authority to take it up again. This charge I have received from My Father.”

units.label: Division over Jesus
units.note: can a demon open the eyes of the blind?

verses.text: Again there was division among the Jews because of Jesus’ message.
Many of them said, “He is demon-possessed and insane. Why would you listen to Him?”
But others replied, “These are not the words of a man possessed by a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?”

units.label: At the Feast of Dedication
units.note: I and the Father are one

verses.text: At that time the Feast of Dedication took place in Jerusalem. It was winter,
and Jesus was walking in the temple courts in Solomon’s Colonnade.
So the Jews gathered around Him and demanded, “How long will You keep us in suspense? If You are the Christ, tell us plainly.”
“I already told you,” Jesus replied, “but you did not believe. The works I do in My Father’s name testify on My behalf.
But because you are not My sheep, you refuse to believe.
My sheep listen to My voice; I know them, and they follow Me.
I give them {{zoe|eternal life}}, and they will never perish. No one can snatch them out of My hand.
My Father who has given them to Me is greater than all. No one can snatch them out of My Father’s hand.
I and the Father are one.”
At this, the Jews again picked up stones to stone Him.
But Jesus responded, “I have shown you many good works from the Father. For which of these do you stone Me?”
“We are not stoning You for any good work,” said the Jews, “but for blasphemy, because You, who are a man, make Yourself out to be God.”
Jesus replied, “Is it not written in your Law: ‘I have said you are gods’?
If he called them gods to whom the word of God came, and the Scripture cannot be broken,
then what about the One whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world? How then can you accuse Me of blasphemy for stating that I am the Son of God?
If I am not doing the works of My Father, then do not believe Me.
But if I am doing them, even though you do not believe Me, believe the works themselves, so that you may know and understand that the Father is in Me, and I am in the Father.”
At this, they tried again to seize Him, but He escaped their grasp.
Then Jesus went back across the Jordan to the place where John had first been baptizing, and He stayed there.
Many came to Him and said, “Although John never performed a sign, everything he said about this man was true.”
And many in that place believed in Jesus.

egoeimi.gloss: I am. Two more of the great I am sayings appear here, I am the gate and I am the good shepherd. As elsewhere in John, the phrase both completes a rich image and quietly carries the resonance of the divine name, reaching its sharpest point in the claim that Jesus and the Father are one, which His hearers rightly take as a claim to deity.

thura.gloss: Door, gate. Jesus is the gate for the sheep: the only true entrance to salvation, safety, and pasture. To enter through Him is to be saved; all who bypass Him and climb in another way are thieves and robbers. The image insists that access to God and His flock is found in Christ alone.

poimen.gloss: Shepherd. Against the false shepherds of Israel condemned by the prophets, Jesus is the good shepherd who knows His sheep by name and lays down His life for them. The image draws on God as the shepherd of His people and on the promise of a coming Davidic shepherd; Jesus fulfills both, tending, gathering, and dying for the flock.

zoe.gloss: Life, eternal life. Jesus came that the sheep may have life in all its fullness, and He gives them eternal life so that they will never perish. This life is held securely, for no one can snatch the sheep from His hand or the Father's; the gift of life is inseparable from the safety of the flock in the shepherd's keeping.

basic.context: After the false shepherds of Israel have just thrown a healed man out of the synagogue, Jesus describes the true shepherd, whose sheep know his voice and follow him. He then applies it: He is the gate through which the sheep are saved, and the good shepherd who lays down His life for them, unlike the hired hand who flees. He speaks of other sheep to be gathered into one flock. Later, at the winter Feast of Dedication, the leaders press Him to say plainly if He is the Christ. He points to His works, promises His sheep can never be snatched away, and says, I and the Father are one. They take up stones for blasphemy.
basic.hermeneutics: The shepherd imagery is loaded with Old Testament meaning: God is Israel's shepherd, the leaders were false shepherds, and a coming David would shepherd the flock. Jesus claims all of it. The key questions are, who is the true shepherd, and how safe are His sheep. Jesus answers that He alone is the door and the shepherd, that He dies willingly and rises, that His sheep are utterly secure in His hand and the Father's, and that He and the Father are one, a claim to deity His hearers understood exactly.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter is built on two I am sayings. Jesus is the thura, the gate, the only entrance to salvation and pasture, and He is the poimen, the good shepherd, who lays down His life for the sheep. He gives them zoe, eternal life, so that they will never perish, held fast by both the Son and the Father, who are ego eimi, one.
basic.typology: Jesus fulfills the picture of God as the shepherd of Israel and the promise of one shepherd, a new David, over the flock. He is the true shepherd against the false shepherds condemned by the prophets, and He gathers the scattered and the other sheep, the nations, into one flock.
basic.christ: Christ is the gate and the good shepherd, who knows His sheep and lays down His life for them of His own accord, with authority to take it up again. He gives eternal life and keeps His sheep unsnatchable. He claims oneness with the Father, an unmistakable claim to deity.
basic.god: God is the shepherd of His people, now present in the Son. The Father gives the sheep to the Son, holds them in His hand, and loves the Son for laying down His life. The Father and the Son are one in keeping the flock secure forever.
basic.crossReferences: Ezekiel 34 condemns false shepherds and promises God and a Davidic shepherd. Psalm 23 sings of the LORD as shepherd. Isaiah 40 pictures God tending His flock. 1 Peter 5 calls Christ the chief Shepherd.
basic.oneStory: The prophets promised that God Himself would come to shepherd His scattered flock and raise up one shepherd from David's line. In Jesus both come true: the good shepherd lays down His life, gathers one flock from many folds, and keeps His sheep forever, for He and the Father are one.

context.literary:
John 10 opens without a scene change, and that is the first thing to see. There is no new setting between 9:41 and 10:1, and 'Truly, truly' simply continues the speech that ended with the Pharisees' guilt. The shepherd discourse is therefore the second half of the story of the man born blind. The thieves and strangers of verses 1 to 5 are the leaders who just threw him out, and the sheep who know a voice are the man who has just heard Jesus say 'You have already seen Him'. Verse 21 closes the circle by recalling the opened eyes.

The chapter has three layers. Verses 1 to 5 give the picture, which John calls a paroimia, a figure of speech, rather than the word parabole the other Gospels use; verse 6 notes that the hearers did not understand it. Verses 7 to 18 then unfold the picture in two stages, each introduced by 'I am': the gate, 7 to 10, and the good shepherd, 11 to 18. Verses 19 to 21 record the division it caused, and verses 22 to 42 move to a second scene, the Feast of Dedication, where the same themes become a direct question about identity.

The two I am sayings are not redundant. The gate is about access and the shepherd is about relationship. Each ends with a statement about life: 'life, and have it in all its fullness', verse 10, and 'I lay down My life', verse 11. Within the second half, the sequence of the shepherd's actions moves from knowing to dying to rising to gathering, verses 14 to 18, and the oneness of the Father and the Son in verse 30 answers the question about knowing that began in verse 14, 'just as the Father knows Me and I know the Father'.

Two details of structure are easy to miss. First, the word 'voice' frames the whole discourse, in verses 3, 4, 5, 16 and 27, and the sheep are defined by what they hear. Second, the chapter ends where John 1 began, with John the Baptist, verses 40 to 42. 'Everything he said about this man was true', and the Book of Signs ends with testimony fulfilled.
context.historical:
Shepherding was the daily life of Israel's ancestors, and its images ran through their language about God and kings. Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses and David were all shepherds, and a king was routinely called the shepherd of his people. A first-century hearer in Judea would have known what it looked like when several flocks were kept overnight in a common walled enclosure under a doorkeeper, and when each shepherd came in the morning and called out his own sheep. The detail that a shepherd calls his sheep by name and leads from the front, verses 3 and 4, matches the practice of the region, where sheep follow a familiar voice rather than being driven.

The scene is not a pastoral idyll. In the Old Testament the leaders of the nation are the shepherds, and the prophets condemned them. Jeremiah 23:1-4 and Ezekiel 34 rebuke the shepherds who feed themselves and scatter the flock, and Zechariah 11 speaks of a worthless shepherd who abandons the sheep. The Pharisees who have just driven the blind man out of the synagogue are the living examples. Jesus does not need to name them.

Verse 22 shifts the setting. The Feast of Dedication, or Hanukkah, fell in winter and commemorated the cleansing of the temple and the rededication of the altar after Antiochus Epiphanes had desecrated it, an event recorded in 1 Maccabees 4, in 164 BC. A feast that celebrated the purifying of the temple and the liberation from foreign rule was also a season when hopes for a deliverer ran high, which is why the crowd presses Jesus in verse 24: 'If You are the Christ, tell us plainly.' He is walking in Solomon's Colonnade, a covered walkway on the eastern side of the temple area, where, according to Acts 3:11 and 5:12, the early church would also gather.

The charge of blasphemy in verse 33 follows the Law's penalty of stoning, Leviticus 24:16. Jesus' reply from Psalm 82 shows He knows exactly what He is being accused of. At the end He withdraws across the Jordan to where John first baptised, a place of beginnings and of safety.
context.canonical:
The Old Testament calls God Israel's shepherd from its earliest pages. Jacob blesses 'the God who has been my shepherd all my life', Genesis 48:15, and the Psalms invoke Him as the Shepherd of Israel, Psalm 80:1, and as the one whose sheep we are, Psalm 100:3. Isaiah promises that 'He tends His flock like a shepherd; He gathers the lambs in His arms', Isaiah 40:11. Under that confession lay a human office: Moses prays for a leader so that the congregation will not be 'like sheep without a shepherd', Numbers 27:17, and David is taken from the sheepfold to shepherd Israel, 2 Samuel 7:8.

The prophets then sharpen the picture into a promise. Ezekiel 34 first condemns the shepherds of Israel and then declares, 'I Myself will search for My flock and seek them out', verse 11, and 'I will appoint over them one shepherd, My servant David', verse 23. John 10 holds both promises at once, because Jesus is both the one who seeks, as God does, and the one appointed, as David's son. Jeremiah 23:3-6 adds the promise of a righteous Branch who will be king. Zechariah 13:7 adds a dark note, 'Strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered', which Jesus will apply to Himself in Matthew 26:31.

Beyond John the picture becomes a title. Hebrews 13:20 calls Jesus 'that great Shepherd of the sheep', brought back from the dead through the blood of the eternal covenant. Peter calls Him the Chief Shepherd, 1 Peter 5:4, and the Shepherd and Overseer of souls, 1 Peter 2:25, and charges the elders to shepherd the flock, 1 Peter 5:2-3. Paul warns the Ephesian elders to guard the flock against savage wolves, Acts 20:28-29. Revelation closes the line with the Lamb as the shepherd who leads His people to springs of living water, Revelation 7:17. In verse 16 the 'other sheep' look forward to the mission to the nations, as in Ephesians 2:13-18 where Jew and Gentile are made one. Verses 34 to 36 draw on Psalm 82:6.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John arranges this chapter to make three claims that his readers needed to hear. First, there is a difference between true and false leadership, and it is not found in office or reputation but in whether one lays down one's life for the flock. The leaders who expelled the man in chapter 9 held every outward qualification and did not care for him. For John's churches, which may have been under the same kind of pressure, the claim was a comfort: those who were put out had a shepherd who knew them.

Second, John wanted to establish that the security of believers rests in the hand of the Son and the Father and not in their own grip. Verses 28 and 29 give a double guarantee, and the repeated 'no one can snatch' meets the fear that persecution or false teaching might take them away. The comfort is not a general mood; it is a pair of hands.

Third, John means the chapter to answer 'if You are the Christ, tell us plainly'. Jesus does not answer with a title but with a claim of oneness with the Father, and John presents the stones that follow as the proof that the claim is understood. The author's aim is to show that everything Jesus did in His good works was an argument for who He is, verses 25, 32 and 37 to 38. A reader who has followed the six signs so far is meant to see the works pointing to the Father in the Son.

The ending also has an aim. Many came and believed beyond the Jordan, verses 41 and 42. After a chapter of stones, John shows that the word still takes root among those who will hear the voice.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The discourse describes who Jesus is and what He does for His own. The sheep are not told to protect themselves, to climb out or to find a way to the pasture; they are given no tasks of rescue at all, and that is the point. They are simply known, called, led and kept. What carries forward is therefore mainly assurance, and the call to listen: 'My sheep listen to My voice', verse 27. The instruction is to hear Christ's voice in His Word, and to follow.

The chapter also describes the failings of false shepherds, and here a careful use is needed. Verse 8, 'All who came before Me were thieves and robbers', is not a condemnation of Moses and the prophets, who spoke of Him, John 5:46, but of those who claimed the leadership of Israel for their own gain. The text describes a pattern of self-serving leadership. It is not a command to treat every pastor with suspicion, nor an excuse for it. The standard it gives to church leaders is a high one, as Peter and Paul understood, 1 Peter 5:2-4 and Acts 20:28.

Verse 18 should be read as describing the unique authority of the Son. Jesus' laying down of His life and His taking it up again are His own work. They are not a template that believers are meant to follow by seeking death or by claiming power over life. Believers are told to love as He loved, 1 John 3:16, but the authority to take life up again is His alone.

Finally, the promise of eternal security is meant to be a comfort and not a licence. Verse 27 describes the sheep as those who listen and follow, which means the promise is given in the company of the call. John does not set the promise against the call, and neither should the reader.

debates.question: Does 'no one can snatch them out of My hand' settle whether a believer can be lost?

views.label: Yes, the sheep are kept absolutely
views.case: The promise is stacked: they will 'never perish', no one can snatch them from the Son's hand, and no one can snatch them from the Father's hand. The same assurance appears in John 6:39 and in Romans 8:38-39. On this view the verse describes those who are truly His sheep and says that nothing outside them, however strong, can take them, and the God who began the work will complete it, Philippians 1:6.

views.label: The promise guards against outside forces, not against a sheep's own departure
views.case: Others note that the verse speaks of what an enemy cannot do, snatch, and not of what a sheep might choose. They point to warnings elsewhere that call believers to continue in the faith, such as Colossians 1:23 and Hebrews 3:12-14, and to the way Jesus ties the promise to hearing and following in verse 27.

debates.bearing: Both sides agree that the verse is addressed to those who hear and follow, and that Christ's grip is stronger than any enemy. They differ over whether following is itself the fruit of being kept or a condition on the keeping. The text gives no ground for anxiety to the one who is listening to the voice, and it gives no ground for presumption to the one who has stopped.

debates.question: What is Jesus doing when He quotes 'I have said you are gods'?

views.label: A lesser to greater argument
views.case: The psalm calls human judges 'gods' because the word of God came to them, Psalm 82:6. If Scripture, which cannot be broken, applies that title to those to whom God's word came, then it is not blasphemy for the one whom the Father sanctified and sent to call Himself the Son of God. The argument is from the lesser to the greater, and it does not reduce His claim to that of a judge.

views.label: A defensive reduction of the claim
views.case: Some take the argument to mean that Jesus is saying only that He is a son of God in the same loose sense as the judges of the psalm, and so is not guilty of blasphemy. They observe that He steps away from the charge of making Himself 'God' and speaks of being the 'Son of God'.

debates.bearing: The surrounding words make the second reading very hard. In verse 30 He says He and the Father are one, and in verse 38 that the Father is in Him and He in the Father. His point in verse 36 is that His case is stronger, not weaker, than that of the psalm's judges: they received the word, He is the One the Father sanctified and sent. The argument shows how He is answering the charge, not that He abandons it.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word that matters is kalos in 'the good shepherd', verses 11 and 14. It is not the plain word agathos, which means morally good, but kalos, which has the sense of good in the sense of excellent, fine or beautiful, the ideal of its kind. A kalos shepherd is the true shepherd, as opposed to the hired man. The adjective is placed after the noun and repeated with the article, 'the shepherd, the good one', which stresses that He is the real thing and not one among many.

The contrast with the hired hand rests on the verb tithemi, 'to lay down', used with psuche, 'life', in verses 11, 15, 17 and 18. The same expression appears when Peter promises to lay down his life, John 13:37, in Jesus' word about the greatest love, John 15:13, and in 1 John 3:16. The idiom is of a voluntary act, not a loss. In verses 17 and 18 the matching verb for 'take up again' is lambano, and the repeated word exousia, 'authority', insists that both laying down and taking up are His own to do. 'No one takes it from Me' is a statement about who is in charge on the cross.

The snatching language is worth noticing. In verse 12 the wolf harpazei the sheep, 'pounces' in the English, and in verses 28 and 29 the same verb harpazo is used of what no one can do to the sheep in the hand of the Son or the Father. The wolf who snatches in verse 12 cannot do what he does in verse 28. The promise 'they will never perish' is built on the strongest Greek negative, ou me, with the verb apollumi, and the words eis ton aiona, 'to the age', which give it a firm 'never, not ever'.

The single most discussed word in the chapter is hen in 'I and the Father are one', verse 30. It is neuter, 'one thing', not the masculine heis, 'one person', which means that Jesus is not saying that He and the Father are the same person. The verb is plural, esmen, 'we are', which the early church, in answering those who collapsed Father and Son into one person, saw as a sign that two are intended. The sentence declares a unity of being and of act, and the stones show the hearers heard it that way.

The scene of verse 16 distinguishes aule, 'fold' or enclosure, from poimne, 'flock'. The other sheep are not of this 'fold', but they will become one 'flock'. There will be one flock and one shepherd, and the unity is found in the shepherd, not in a shared pen. Finally, the verb hagiazo in verse 36, 'sanctified', is the one used of setting apart for God's service, and it is a strong word to use at the Feast of the Dedication, when the altar was set apart again.

typology.type: David the shepherd who risked his life
typology.fulfillment: David defended his father's sheep against a lion and a bear, 1 Samuel 17:34-36, and told Saul that he went after the beast and struck it, 1 Samuel 17:35. That is the Old Testament picture of a shepherd who stands between the flock and the predator. God then took him from the sheepfold to shepherd Israel, 2 Samuel 7:8. The correspondence with Jesus is exact in its pattern and goes far beyond it in its cost: David risked his life and survived, while Jesus lays His life down and takes it up again, John 10:17-18. The type falls short because David's kingdom fell into failure and exile, while the Son's shepherding ends in one flock under one shepherd.

typology.type: The LORD who Himself shepherds His flock
typology.fulfillment: Ezekiel 34 promises that God will personally seek the lost, bring back the strays and bind up the broken, verses 11 and 16, and also promises one shepherd, My servant David, verse 23. The shepherds of Israel had abandoned their duty, and Jesus draws the contrast with the hired hand in verses 12 and 13. In Jesus both the promise of God Himself and the promise of David's son are met in one Person. The escalation is that the divine shepherd comes in the flesh and lays down His life for the flock. The type is not exhausted, for Revelation 7:17 still looks ahead to a day when the Lamb will shepherd His people to springs of living water.

Psalm 118:20 says, 'This is the gate of the LORD; the righteous shall enter through it', and Jacob at Bethel called the place the house of God and the gate of heaven, Genesis 28:17. Jesus takes the place of the gate. Anyone who enters through Him will be saved and will go in and out and find pasture, verse 9, which echoes the shepherd's work of leading the people out and bringing them in, Numbers 27:17. The correspondence is that the way into God's presence is no longer a place but a Person. The escalation is that the gate is not guarded to exclude but opened by the shepherd Himself, and the type falls short in that earlier gates were entered by obedience, while this one is entered by trust.

typology.type: The Feast of Dedication and the consecrated Son
typology.fulfillment: The feast recalled the cleansing of the temple and the setting apart of its altar again for God, as told in 1 Maccabees 4. Jesus speaks at that very feast of 'the One whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world', verse 36. The temple was once rededicated by human hands; here God's own consecrated One walks in the temple. The correspondence is the idea of a place and a person set apart for God, and the escalation is that the true dwelling of God is the Son in whom the Father is, verse 38, as John 2:19-21 has already said. The type falls short because the rededicated altar served a building that would again be destroyed.

study.christ:
The chapter presents Christ in His authority, His love and His oneness with the Father, and it does so by means of a person who is both gate and shepherd. As the gate He is the only access, and this is a statement of exclusivity said with great warmth. Whoever enters through Him will be saved, will come in and go out, and will find pasture, verse 9. The good that the gate secures is not a narrow safety but liberty and nourishment. Alongside the plain words of John 14:6, the gate says that the way to the Father runs through the Son.

As the shepherd He is set against the thief who comes to steal, kill and destroy, and the hired hand who flees. The distinctive mark of this shepherd is that He dies for the sheep, and the chapter says again and again that He lays down His life, verses 11, 15, 17 and 18. The cross is not a defeat that interrupts His shepherding but the act of it. Isaiah 53:6 had said that all of us like sheep have gone astray and that the LORD laid on Him the iniquity of us all. Zechariah 13:7 and Jesus' use of it in Matthew 26:31 add that the Shepherd must be struck. And the shepherd does not stay struck: 'I have authority to lay it down and authority to take it up again', verse 18. Hebrews 13:20 holds the two together, calling Him the great Shepherd, brought back from the dead.

The intimacy of His knowledge is another part of the portrait. 'I know My sheep and My sheep know Me, just as the Father knows Me and I know the Father', verses 14 and 15. The knowledge between Jesus and His people is set beside the knowledge between the Son and the Father. That is an astonishing comparison. It does not say that the sheep know Him as God knows Him, but that there is a real relationship of knowing, rooted in the Trinity's own life. It echoes the prayer that believers may be one as the Father and the Son are one, John 17:11 and 22.

The security He gives rests on who He is. The sheep are in His hand, and the Father's hand is also the sheep's, and then He says, 'I and the Father are one.' The oneness is the ground of the security. A shepherd who is merely a good man might fail, but one who is one with the Father cannot be overpowered.

The chapter also leads Christ's mission outward. 'I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them in as well', verse 16. The word 'must' shows the necessity of the cross for the gathering of the nations, and it prepares for the saying in 11:52 about the scattered children of God and for the Greeks who come to see Him in 12:20-24.

A caution keeps the reading faithful. Not every detail of shepherding, such as the doorkeeper of verse 3, needs a counterpart. Jesus Himself identifies only the gate, the shepherd and the thieves, and the rest should be read as the setting of the picture.
study.god:
This chapter says more about the inner life of God than almost any other passage in the Gospel of John, and it says it in the language of a shepherd. First, God is a seeker and a keeper. The Old Testament promise that the LORD Himself will search for His sheep, Ezekiel 34:11, is fulfilled in the Son who calls His own by name and leads them out. The attributes revealed are care for individuals, the knowledge of each by name, and the readiness to go ahead of them. It is the opposite of the distant deity.

Second, the Father is the source and the guarantor of the sheep's safety. 'My Father who has given them to Me is greater than all,' verse 29. The sheep are a gift from the Father to the Son, and the Father's hand is joined to the Son's in holding them. The security of the flock does not rest on the sheep's strength or on the shepherd's alone; it rests on the one God who is both Father and Son. This is why the passage is a rich text for the doctrine of God. The Father gives, the Son keeps, and the unity of the two is what makes the keeping unbreakable.

Third, the Father loves the Son for His self-giving. 'The reason the Father loves Me is that I lay down My life in order to take it up again,' verse 17. This does not mean that the Father's love began when the Son obeyed. John 17:24 speaks of the Father loving the Son before the foundation of the world. It means that the Son's willing death and rising is the expression of the shared purpose within God, and that the Father delights in it. The cross is not a transaction forced on an unwilling party. It is a charge received from the Father, verse 18, and gladly carried out by the Son.

Fourth, God is one in being while distinct in persons. 'I and the Father are one', and 'the Father is in Me, and I am in the Father', verses 30 and 38. These words do not say that the Father and the Son are the same person, and they do not say that they are merely agreed. The Gospel is giving the language that the church will later use of one God in more than one person. The passage does not state the doctrine of the Trinity in so many words, but it is the kind of text from which the doctrine was drawn.

Fifth, God's justice is shown in the way He deals with the false shepherds. The prophets promised that the LORD would judge them, Ezekiel 34:10, and the chapter shows the beginning of that judgment: the thieves are exposed by the contrast with the shepherd. God's care for the flock and His anger at those who exploit it are the same love seen from two sides.

For worship, the chapter calls for trust and for listening. To hear a voice and follow is the posture of praise. The believer who knows that the Father is greater than all, and that the sheep are held in two hands, can rest. The God we worship is not only majestic but near, and His nearness has been shown in a Shepherd who knows our name.

crossReferences.note: God says He Himself will search for His flock and seek them out. Jesus' words in verses 11 to 16 take up this promise, and His seeking of the man He found in 9:35 is an example of it. The divine shepherd of Ezekiel is here a person in Jerusalem.

God promises to appoint one shepherd, His servant David. This is the other half of the promise, which Jesus meets as David's heir. John 10:16 speaks of one shepherd and one flock, which is the language of Ezekiel 34:23 and 37:24.

Moses prays for a leader who will lead the people out and bring them in, so that they will not be like sheep without a shepherd. Jesus' shepherd leads the sheep out in verse 3 and says they will go in and out and find pasture in verse 9, so the Old Testament prayer is answered in Him.

The gate of the LORD is the place where the righteous enter. By calling Himself the gate in verses 7 and 9, Jesus puts Himself in the place of the entrance to God's presence, an entrance the psalm marks for the righteous.

The LORD calls for the sword against His Shepherd, whom He calls the man who is His Companion, and the sheep are scattered. Jesus quotes the passage on the night of His arrest, Matthew 26:31. It shows that the shepherd's death was foretold, and that verse 18 is not a surprise.

The psalm addresses human judges with the words 'You are gods'. Jesus uses it in verses 34 to 36 to answer the charge of blasphemy and to argue from the lesser to the greater. The reference is brief, but it shows how closely He reads the Law.

Jesus says that the Father's will is that He lose none of those given to Him. This expresses the same security as verse 28 and joins it to the last day: those the Father gives are raised up. The two passages interpret each other.

Jesus prays that the Father will protect His own so that they may be one as the Father and the Son are one. It repeats the word 'one' of verse 30 and shows that the unity of the Father and the Son is the pattern and the source of the unity of the flock.

Paul tells the elders at Ephesus to shepherd the church of God, which He obtained with His own blood, and warns of savage wolves. Paul's wolves are the wolf of verse 12, and the elders are being asked to be shepherds and not hired hands.

The God of peace brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great Shepherd of the sheep. The verse unites the death of verse 11 with the rising of verse 18 and presents both as the shepherd's work.

The Lamb in the center of the throne will be the shepherd of His people, leading them to springs of living water. The picture of the shepherd who dies is completed in the Lamb who reigns and who shepherds the great multitude.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a man given a garden to tend and keep, Genesis 2:15, and the question of who will keep the flock of God's people runs from there through the whole story. After the fall humanity is scattered and without a keeper. Abel is a keeper of sheep, Genesis 4:2, and his blood is the first to cry out. Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses and David are shepherds called to lead God's people, and each leads them in some part and fails in some part. Israel's story of exile is the story of what happens when the shepherds feed themselves: the flock is scattered, as Ezekiel 34:5-6 says.

Into that history God makes His promise. He Himself will come, and He will appoint one shepherd over them. The prophets never explain how the two promises become one, and the story waits. John 10 is the place where the waiting ends. The shepherd who is God and the shepherd who is David's heir are one man, who stands in the temple at winter and says that He knows His sheep and gives His life for them.

The chapter also draws out a thread that has been in the story from the start, the thread of the nations. God promised Abraham that all families of the earth would be blessed, Genesis 12:3, and the 'other sheep' of verse 16 are that promise coming to rest. Jew and Gentile are brought into one flock under one shepherd, and this is the great work of the church, which Paul calls the one new humanity, Ephesians 2:15.

The shepherd's death is placed at the middle of the story, and its cost is made clear. Isaiah's servant was led like a lamb to the slaughter, Isaiah 53:7, and in Jesus the shepherd and the lamb are the same. When the story ends, the images join: 'the Lamb in the center of the throne will be their shepherd', Revelation 7:17, and 'God will wipe away every tear from their eyes'. The garden that was lost is replaced by the city and the pasture, and the flock that was scattered is gathered. The promise of verse 28 is the promise of the whole story. They will never perish, for the shepherd has been struck, has risen, and holds them in a hand that no enemy can open.

quiz.q: What does Jesus mean by saying I am the gate for the sheep?

options.text: He is the only true entrance to salvation, safety, and pasture; whoever enters through Him is saved.
options.note: Verse 9 ties entering through Him to being saved and finding pasture.

options.text: He is one of several ways people may come to God.
options.note: The image insists He is the gate; all who bypass Him are thieves and robbers.

options.text: He guards the sheep by standing at the entrance.
options.note: He does protect the flock, but the claim is that He Himself is the only door of salvation.

options.text: He is the way into God's flock and its safe pasture.
options.note: True, but it softens the exclusive claim that anyone saved must enter through Him alone.

quiz.q: What distinguishes the good shepherd from the hired hand?

options.text: The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep, while the hired hand flees when the wolf comes.
options.note: Verses 11 to 13 contrast the shepherd's self-sacrifice with the hireling's flight.

options.text: The good shepherd owns more sheep than the hired hand.
options.note: The difference is love and sacrifice, not the size of the flock.

options.text: The good shepherd knows the sheep and cares for them.
options.note: True, but it omits the decisive mark, that He lays down His life for them.

options.text: The good shepherd is paid more for his work.
options.note: The point is the opposite of hire; He gives His life freely, not for wages.

quiz.q: How secure are Jesus' sheep, according to verses 28 and 29?

options.text: They have eternal life, will never perish, and no one can snatch them from His hand or the Father's.
options.note: Verses 28 and 29 promise complete security in the hands of the Son and the Father.

options.text: They are safe only as long as they hold on tightly enough.
options.note: Their security rests on the shepherd's grip, not their own strength.

options.text: They are kept safe in the Father's hand.
options.note: True, but it leaves out that they are equally held in the Son's hand and given eternal life that never perishes.

options.text: They are protected from most dangers but not all.
options.note: The promise is absolute: no one can snatch them away, not a partial safety.

quiz.q: Why did the crowd pick up stones after Jesus said I and the Father are one?

options.text: Because they understood Him to be claiming to be God, which they called blasphemy.
options.note: Verse 33 states they stoned Him for making Himself out to be God.

options.text: Because He had broken the Sabbath again.
options.note: Sabbath was an earlier charge; here the explicit issue is His claim to be one with the Father.

options.text: Because He refused to answer whether He was the Christ.
options.note: He did answer, pointing to His works and His oneness with the Father.

options.text: Because He claimed a unique unity with the Father.
options.note: True, but it does not name that they specifically charged Him with blasphemy for making Himself God.

quiz.q: What does Jesus say about the other sheep not of this fold?

options.text: He must bring them in too, so there will be one flock and one shepherd.
options.note: Verse 16 anticipates the gathering of others into a single flock under Him.

options.text: They will always remain separate from His flock.
options.note: The opposite; He will bring them in to form one flock.

options.text: They are other Jewish believers not yet gathered in.
options.note: The other sheep most likely include the Gentiles, not only scattered Jews; either way Jesus gathers them into one flock.

options.text: They will also hear His voice and follow Him.
options.note: True, but it omits the goal, one flock and one shepherd.

questions: Jesus says His sheep know His voice. How well do you recognize His voice amid the many voices competing for your attention?
The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep of His own accord. How does it move you that Christ's death was a free gift of love, not a defeat forced on Him?
No one can snatch Jesus' sheep from His hand. Where do you need the comfort of that security today?
Jesus came to give life in all its fullness, against the thief who steals and destroys. Where are you settling for a thin, robbed life instead of the fullness He offers?
Jesus gathers other sheep into one flock. How does His heart for those still outside shape the way you pray for and reach people far from Him?

translationNotes.note: The Feast of Dedication; the BSB footnote explains this is Hanukkah, celebrating the Maccabean rededication of the temple. It is a fitting backdrop as Jesus speaks of being sanctified and sent by the Father.
I have said you are gods quotes Psalm 82:6, addressed to human judges; Jesus argues from the lesser to the greater to answer the charge of blasphemy.
The Scripture cannot be broken affirms the unbreakable authority of Scripture, on which Jesus rests His argument.
One flock and one shepherd; the other sheep not of this fold anticipate the gathering of the Gentiles into one people under Christ.
